item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Monday briefing: How the new phase of confrontation at al-Aqsa signals a challenge to the status quo
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: ​Jerusalem’s most volatile site has again become a flashpoint, with Arab states and former Israeli officials sounding the alarm over Benjamin Netanyahu’s complicity

Good morning. In late July, Itamar Ben-Gvir, West Bank settler and far-right extremist minister of security in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, joined a group of more than 2,000 Jewish extremists to storm al-Aqsa mosque compound, Jerusalem’s most sensitive holy site. The far-right group has been doing this for years. Ben-Gvir has made series of visits to the site over the last three years, eroding norms and inflaming tensions. Jordanian officials have recently warned that it could be at risk of an “imminent” Israeli takeover.

With national elections scheduled in October, and many eyes still firmly on Gaza (this weekend, Netanyahu rejected a US-backed 15 point plan for peace), the Israeli government appears to be racing to expand Israeli settlements and accelerate ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem before its mandate expires.

UK politics | Sadiq Khan has called on the government to commit to revamped climate action and to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas, as the UK endures a summer of drought, wildfires and heatwaves.

US politics | The US Senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus.

US-Israel war on Iran | Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.

Russia-Ukraine | Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. On Saturday, Turkey called for a “moratorium” on attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea after a series of strikes on civilian ships there

World news | The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group was extradited from Dubai on Sunday and met by a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat and mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities.

Wednesday | A partial solar eclipse will be visible across the whole of the UK, with the south-west of England getting the best of British views. Parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain will experience a total eclipse.

Thursday | Clacton-on-sea residents will vote in the byelection Nigel Farage triggered last month, with the Reform leader taking on 33 mostly novelty candidates. Results are expected early Friday.

item.description:
Trump says Iran must pay compensation for those it has killed and wounded

US President Donald Trump said on Monday he will demand that Iran pay compensation for "all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded", in response to Iran seeking compensation for the damages it has incurred from US and Israeli attacks.

Trump's social media post came after Iran said over the weekend it was nearing a deal with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz, but repeated that the US must meet conditions including compensation and an end to sanctions and military threats, before the strategic waterway is reopened.

"It is an interesting idea because now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts," he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump also referenced and claimed compensation from Iran for the October 2000 deadly bombing of the US Navy guided-missile destroyer USS Cole at a Yemeni port. The FBI has attributed that bombing, which killed 17 sailors and wounded more than three dozen others, to al-Qaeda.

Trump added that Tehran should also pay compensation to the families of the thousands of people killed during anti-government protests in January, Iran's worst domestic unrest since the era of its 1979 Islamic Revolution.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] UAE's Adnoc announces $8bn gas expansion, as it mulls Hormuz bypass
item.description:
UAE's Adnoc announces $8bn gas expansion, as it mulls Hormuz bypass

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 08/10/2026 - 18:39
The UAE could be the first country to plan a gas pipeline bypassing the Strait of Hormuz
Sultan Ahmed al-Jaber, the UAE's minister of industry and advanced technology, Adnoc managing director and group CEO, and chairman of the Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company 'Masdar', attends the fifth edition of the 'Make it in the Emirates' conference in Abu Dhabi, on 4 May 4 2026 (Fadel Senna/AFP)
Off

The UAE’s state-owned energy giant, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc), said on Monday it will invest $8bn to expand its gas business, doubling down on increasing capacity after the Gulf state pulled out of the Saudi Arabian-led energy alliance, Opec.

Adnoc said it plans to build a new domestic natural gas processing unit at the country’s largest natural gas processing facility, Habshan, in addition to a new gas export facility at Ruwais.

Separately, Adnoc Gas’s CFO, Peter van Driel, told Bloomberg on Monday that the company was also weighing plans to build a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facility outside the Strait of Hormuz. That facility would be in addition to the facility at Ruwais that Adnoc Gas is building to more than double its export capacity to about 15 million tonnes a year.

The move comes at a time when the Gulf’s LNG powerhouse, Qatar, has declared a force majeure on LNG shipments through the autumn as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Qatar relies on vessels to ship gas in liquefied form.  

Iran and the US are locked in negotiations over the status of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical corridor through which roughly 25 percent of the world’s energy passes.

Qatar resumed some LNG shipments after the US and Iran extended a ceasefire in June, but Qatari vessels have been attacked while transiting Oman’s territorial waters in recent months.

The UAE’s vessels have also been struck by Iran, but the Gulf state has taken a more risk-prone approach to sending vessels through the Strait of Hormuz with their ship tracking signals turned off.

Reuters reported in June that the UAE paid Iran billions of dollars in return for a halt to attacks on the country, in an about-face for the Gulf state that launched dozens of attacks on Iran alongside the US and Israel during the war.

The UAE has also benefited from an oil pipeline that terminates at Fujairah, outside the Strait of Hormuz. 

Exclusive: Syria, Iraq and US plan to unveil Mediterranean pipeline deal to bypass Strait of Hormuz
Read More »

That pipeline has helped the UAE continue exporting oil even as other Gulf states, such as Kuwait and Bahrain, are effectively locked out of the market.

The UAE boosted oil production to an all-time high in June, pumping 4.1 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in a report released in July.

Like the UAE, Saudi Arabia has the East-West Pipeline, which bypasses the Strait of Hormuz via the Red Sea.

Experts told Middle East Eye that tens of billions of dollars will be spent on new infrastructure in the coming years to get around Hormuz. 

“When we speak to our customers in the region, they say they never want to deal with this again,” Artem Abramov, the deputy head of analysis at Rystad Energy, previously told MEE. “These bypass projects will move forward.”

The UAE is building a second pipeline to the port of Fujairah to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, doubling its export capacity by 2027.

Meanwhile, Iraq - the second-largest producer in the oil cartel Opec - signed a deal with Syria in July to rehabilitate a pipeline from its northern oil fields to Syria’s Mediterranean coast. MEE was the first to reveal the project and its US backing

The UAE’s surging production also reflects analysts' assessments that Abu Dhabi long felt constrained by Saudi-led Opec. The UAE has invested heavily in boosting its production capacity but complained for years that Saudi Arabia, in a bid to support prices, had stopped it from producing more. The UAE left Opec in May 2026.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Trump asks Iran for war reparations in new tit-for-tat demand
item.description:
Trump asks Iran for war reparations in new tit-for-tat demand

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 08/10/2026 - 21:35
The US president has established a pattern of asking Iran for its own demands, even as aides and allies attack their validity
During an event in the Oval Office of the White House, US President Donald Trump takes a question from reporters after he signed an executive order calling for childhood vaccine shots to be spaced out into separate visits, on 10 August 2026 in Washington, DC (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

US President Donald Trump said on Monday he would seek compensation from Iran for the deaths of US soldiers as part of any peace negotiations in a tit-for-tat demand after Tehran requested war reparations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. 

“I see that Representatives of the Islamic Republic of Iran are asking for compensation for the damage done to them during the last five-month Military Conflict (started because, THEY WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON), even though it was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran," he added.

Trump said he wanted reparations not only from damages arising from the current war, but also attacks Iran is widely believed to have facilitated through allied militias on US soldiers going back more than two decades after the 2003 US invasion of Iraq.

Trump referenced the deaths and injuries of US soldiers from roadside bombs that Iranian General Qassem Soleimani is believed to have orchestrated. Iran began arming Shia militias with roadside bombs in the mid-2000s during the US occupation of Iraq.

The campaign was part of Iran and the US’s battle for influence in Iraq. Trump ordered the assassination of Soleimani inside Iraq in 2020, citing his role in supporting militias aligned with Tehran.

Trump’s post also cited the October 2000 bombing of the USS Cole warship, but US intelligence agencies have blamed al-Qaeda for the attack, not Tehran.

Iran says it is not concerned by new 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement'
Read More »

Trump also requested that Iran pay its own citizens compensation for the death of protesters at the start of the year. Trump partially justified the February 2026 US and Israeli war on Iran by citing its crackdown on protesters.

Trump said 50,000 people were killed, while an Iranian official put the number at at least 5,000 people.

It’s unclear how serious Trump is about conditioning a ceasefire on compensation for the death of US service members, let alone Iranian nationals. But his comments came after Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Iran needed war reparations in order to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump’s rebuttal fits a pattern of him matching Iranian demands with his own.

The US president contradicted his own secretary of state, Marco Rubio, in July when he said that the US could charge a toll of 20 percent in the Strait of Hormuz in return for being its “guardian”.

Rubio has insisted that any toll in the waterway is “completely illegal”.

Trump’s latest post underscores how a ceasefire extension between the two sides announced in June has effectively broken down, as Washington and Tehran look for an advantage on the battlefield.

However, The Wall Street Journal reported over the weekend that Trump had effectively given up on his main stated objective when he started the war - ensuring a nuclear agreement with Tehran that prevents it from pursuing a path to a nuclear weapon. The report said Trump would end the war in order to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Less than four percent of US safety funding went to Muslim institutions: Report
item.description:
Less than four percent of US safety funding went to Muslim institutions: Report

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 08/10/2026 - 20:36
Nearly 60 percent of the Department of Homeland Security’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program went to Jewish nonprofits
Muslims embrace in the parking lot of the Islamic Center of San Diego after three people were killed in a shooting at the city’s largest mosque, in San Diego, California on 19 May 19 2026 (Sandy Huffaker/Getty Images via AFP)
Off

Over the past decade in the US, since Donald Trump first ascended to the White House in 2017, less than four percent of US government grant funding to keep religious institutions safe has gone to Muslim nonprofits, a new report by the Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC) has found.

The funds are awarded annually through the Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP), which is operated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). 

An institution can typically receive a maximum of some $200,000 for each site it operates, and the money must be put toward physical safeguards: security cameras, bulletproof glass, guardrails around properties, and the training of security guards, among other tools. 

Nearly 60 percent of the pot has gone to Jewish groups, followed by Christian groups at a little over 25 percent, the figures in the report showed. 

"Of the $850m awarded through this program over nine years, Muslim organisations only got 3.8 percent of the funding... it's a really, really small amount going to a community that is under threat, and a growing threat," Dr Sarah Mohamed, a co-author of the report and a senior researcher with MPAC's Center for Security, Technology, and Policy, told Middle East Eye on Monday.

A year ago, the conservative think tank, Middle East Forum, published a report claiming that DHS was using US tax dollars to fund "terror-linked and extremist groups" between 2013 and 2023.

That report listed 49 Muslim-American organisations, and said the NSGP "remains the greatest source of DHS funding to extremist groups". 

"Even members of Congress have not been able to verify that," Sameer Hossein, MPAC's managing director in Washington, DC, and the other author of the report, told MEE.

"What we do know for sure is that the terms and conditions that DHS has put out for this year and the previous year under the current administration make it even more difficult for American Muslims and other community organisations to apply for these very critical grants," he added.

That's because the administration has been cracking down on initiatives that go against its policy platform: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI); assistance to undocumented immigrants; and boycotts of Israel.

"If you as a grantee were found to be engaging in those prohibited activities, you expose yourself to more legal risk," Hossein said. 

So was the limited funding for Muslim groups inevitable, given the current political climate? That's not certain, Mohamed said.

"We don't have any public information about how many institutions applied. So the denominator isn't available for us to be able to say [that]," she told MEE.

MPAC has engaged with Jewish-American groups on the issue, Hossein noted, and they tend to be better resourced and practised at the cumbersome and bureaucratic process of applying for the grant, he said.

Jewish nonprofits were among the first to request a programme like NSGP, following the establishment of DHS, in the wake of the 9/11 attacks. 

Anti-Muslim sentiment on the rise

Anti-Muslim sentiment in the US has skyrocketed since the Trump administration assumed power in January 2025.

The president's agenda, largely pre-orchestrated by the far-right Heritage Foundation in its Project 2025 document, puts Muslim-American communities and Muslim countries in the crosshairs.

Republican lawmakers have openly derided Muslims and called for legal action or violence against them - most notoriously Florida Congressman Randy Fine, Tennessee Congressman Andy Ogles, and Alabama Senator Tommy Tuberville. 

Trump himself recently shared an image of a group of Minnesota Muslim kindergarteners in hijabs to his Truth Social platform, where he has often called for Somali Americans in the state to be investigated and deported, including hijab-wearing Congresswoman Ilhan Omar.

In the lead-up to the election of the very first Muslim mayor of New York City last year, The Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH) revealed in a 20-page document that Islamophobic and xenophobic discourse surrounding Zohran Mamdani on X had a reach of some 1.5 billion between his Democratic primary win in June and the end of October. 

Anti-Muslim lawmaker Andy Ogles loses Republican primary
Read More »

The organisation called on the platform to implement election-specific safeguards, enforce community guidelines against attacks on race and religion, and enhance corrective counterarguments in its algorithm. 

CSOH also reported a sharp increase in anti-Muslim content on X since Israel and the US launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February.

The Washington, DC-based social media monitor said it tracked posts that explicitly dehumanised, excluded, and incited violence against Muslims from 1 January to 5 March, during which Trump was consistently threatening to start the war.

On the day the war began, the volume of such posts surged from just under 2,000 per day to more than 6,000, the report said. 

In April, MPAC revealed that attacks on Muslim-American individuals and institutions were at a 15-month high under the Trump administration.

The group documented an eleven-fold increase in targeted incidents in the first three months of this year alone.

At least nine of the attacks occurred in March, ranging from vandalism and bomb threats at mosques to sexual assaults against Muslim women, according to a policy paper entitled "The Pitfalls of Operation Epic Fury: How the Undeclared War Against Iran Hurts Americans’ Interests Abroad and at Home."

In May, after a shooting that killed three people outside a California mosque that housed a school with children inside, Muslim-American groups blamed what they said was the mainstreaming of anti-Muslim hate speech by lawmakers and other right-wing influential figures. 

"We are deeply disturbed, but not at all surprised," the Council on American-Islamic Relations said in a statement at the time. "Hate against American Muslims is completely out of control."

Now, with Michigan Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed potentially on his way to becoming the first-ever Muslim US senator in the country's history, his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, has released an attack ad on Sayed featuring images of Osama bin Laden.

item.description:
Jennifer Balkcom to face Democrat Jamie Ager in race to represent North Carolina’s 11th congressional district

North Carolina Republicans on Monday chose state lawmaker Jennifer Balkcom to replace Chuck Edwards, the incumbent congressman who earlier this month dropped his re-election bid after a US House investigation determined his conduct towards to young female staffers likely amounted to sexual harassment.

Balkcom will face off against the Democratic nominee, Jamie Ager, in the November midterm elections to represent the 11th congressional district in western North Carolina. Though Donald Trump won the district by 10 percentage points two years ago, Democrats believe Ager may have a shot at winning amid the president’s low approval ratings and frustration over the pace of recovery from Hurricane Helene, which devastated the region in 2024.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Trump hid in catering cart to board secret flight in Turkey amid Iran threat – reports
item.description:
Elaborate ruse was used to transport president to military flight from Air Force One to return from Nato meet

Prompted by an Iranian assassination threat, Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Turkey last month when the White House said he was flying aboard ⁠Air Force One, in an extraordinary ruse that involved hiding the president in an airport catering cart, according to reporting from the Washington Post and the New York Times.

The operation took place when Trump was in Ankara for a Nato summit with world leaders, according to the Post. The president reportedly boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras, and then was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight, a US official told the Post.

item.description:
Iran says it is not concerned by new 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement'

Iran has played down the mutual security agreement signed between the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey in the Muslim holy city of Mecca on Friday.

Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, said on Monday that Tehran saw no reason to be concerned that a new security pact is directed against Iran.

Baghaei said the pact showed a "change in perception" towards the US, as well as a shift in the regional approach to security.

He added that the agreement represented a shift towards greater reliance on the states' own capabilities rather than outside powers.
